hints: Focus on getting every quantity into the correct SI units before you touch the ideal gas equation.
Convert 60 degrees C to 333 K and 103 kPa to 103000 Pa, then use $n = pV/RT$ to find moles of methane.
Multiply your moles by the molar mass of methane, $M_r = 16.0$, to get mass in grams and round to two significant figures.
walkthrough:
**List data and convert units**

Great start, let's get organised. The ideal gas equation only works with SI units, so temperature must be in kelvin and pressure in pascals.

$$T = 60 + 273 = 333 \text{ K}$$
$$p = 103 \text{ kPa} = 103 \times 10^3 = 103000 \text{ Pa}$$
$$V = 5.37 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$$
$$R = 8.31 \text{ J K}^{-1} \text{ mol}^{-1}$$

**Calculate moles with pV = nRT**

Now rearrange to find moles. Think of it as counting how many gas particles the pressure and volume correspond to.

$$n = \frac{pV}{RT}$$
$$n = \frac{103000 \times 5.37 \times 10^{-3}}{8.31 \times 333}$$
$$n = \frac{553.11}{2767.23} \approx 0.20 \text{ mol}$$

**Convert moles to mass of methane**

Finally, turn moles into grams. Methane is $\text{CH}_4$, so its molar mass is $12.0 + (4 \times 1.0) = 16.0 \text{ g mol}^{-1}$.

$$\text{mass} = n \times M_r$$
$$\text{mass} = 0.1999 \times 16.0 \approx 3.2 \text{ g}$$

options.A: Incorrect. 0.0032 g is 1000 times too small. This happens if you mix up kPa and Pa, or $m^3$ and $dm^3$, so your moles come out a factor of 1000 out.
options.B: Incorrect. 0.018 g is far too small and close to the mole value itself. This trap catches you if you forget to multiply moles by the molar mass of 16.0, or confuse mass with moles.
options.C: Correct. With $n \approx 0.20$ mol and $M_r(\text{CH}_4) = 16.0$, mass $= 0.20 \times 16.0 = 3.2$ g to two significant figures.
options.D: Incorrect. 18 g would be just over 1 mole of methane. This results from using Celsius temperature (60) instead of kelvin (333), which makes the bottom of $pV/RT$ far too small and $n$ far too large.
